item.text: {"text":"NextItNet’s causal dilated convolutions and residual blocks make temporal-order and recency probes architecturally relevant. However, the located literature does not establish that activation-patching effects or training-history memorization diagnostics predict subsequent held-out HR@10 improvements in NextItNet. Activation-patching research primarily supports localization of model behavior, with conclusions sensitive to corruption methods and measurement choices; applying it as a training-selection signal remains an extrapolation. [NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf), [activation-patching methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042).\n\nRecency has stronger adjacent evidence: recency-sampling research studies actionable training changes, while recency-bias research reports performance improvements from mitigating excessive recency dependence. Neither establishes that this proposed diagnostic identifies the right intervention for these four Amazon categories. [Recency sampling](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/299238/), [recency-bias study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722). Practical assessment: exploratory value, insufficient evidence for an optimistic improvement forecast or substantial diagnostic budget. Start with inexpensive temporal perturbations that preserve padding and the final interaction, then test any suggested regularization through controlled single-model retraining and the pinned macro validation HR@10. Treat perturbation sensitivity as behavioral evidence, not proof of memorization. Sampled metrics can reverse model rankings relative to full-catalog evaluation, so diagnostic gains on twenty full-catalog users cannot substitute for the required 99-negative validation objective. [Sampled-metric analysis](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)."}
